# Volume 3 — Chapter XXXVI The Gardners’Call

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Aunt Phemie, a letter bearing an Indian stamp has arrived for you,” Cressy said. “Mabel has three, Nonie has two, and I have a wonderful thick one sent by Ez. Nell, you have received only a circular.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0000 }

No one observed the color rising in Nell's cheeks when she caught the slim envelope that Cressy casually threw to her. Shortly afterwards, however, Cressy raised her eyes and saw that Nell was completely transformed.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0001 }

“Sweetheart, what nice event took place?”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0002 }

“A short piece I transmitted to The Youth’s Friend two weeks back has been taken by them,” stated Nell, attempting with great effort to sound as though she had pieces taken with every post, though failing to fully pull it off.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0003 }

“Nell Harcourt! How wonderful! What was the piece? When will it be printed? Were you paid for it by them?”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0004 }

“Indeed; a check amounting to ten dollars has been dispatched by them, and the editor states in his letter a desire to examine additional pieces of my writing. Kind gentleman, he certainly will. The piece was a former sketch that I discovered inside my trunk. After re-writing it, I submitted it—though I actually held no expectation that it might be taken owing to its lack of plot,” stated Nell, remembering the painful ordeal regarding Evadne’s Atonement.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0005 }

“What will you do with those ten dollars, Nell? How about we all head up town and get drunk,” Cressy proposed.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0006 }

“I intend to waste it on a soulless, wild party of some kind,” Nell cheerfully announced. “Whatever happens, it is not corrupt cash—unlike the payment I received for that awful Reliable Baking Powder tale. I bought needed garments with that money and despised them whenever I wore them.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0007 }

“Imagine hosting an actual living writer at Tabby’s Place,” Honora remarked.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0008 }

“Taking this on involves a significant duty,” Aunt Euphemia remarked with gravity.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0009 }

“Truly, that’s so,” concurred Nonie, matching my gravity. “Writers are tricky creatures. Predicting the time or manner of their outbursts is impossible. It could be that Nell will use us as material.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0010 }

“The capacity to compose material for the Press represented a heavy charge,” Aunt Euphemia stated sternly, “and I trust Nell comprehends this. Prior to departing for the foreign field, my daughter was accustomed to composing tales, yet currently she has directed her mind toward loftier matters. She was wont to remark that her guiding principle was ‘Never write a line you would be ashamed to read at your own funeral.’ It would be wise for you to adopt that as your own, Nell, provided you intend to launch yourself into literature. Although, to be certain,” Aunt Euphemia appended in a puzzled manner, “Elizabeth was in the habit of laughing whenever she uttered those words. She was perpetually laughing to such an extent that I cannot comprehend how she ever arrived at the choice to become a missionary. I am grateful for her decision—I offered prayers that she would—yet—I would prefer that she had not.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0011 }

Aunt Euphemia then inquired about the reason for the laughter of those silly young women.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0012 }

Nell’s eyes gleamed throughout that entire day; literary aspirations began to grow and flourish within her mind; the excitement of them went along with her to Jennie Cooper’s walking party, and even seeing Hugh and Rowena, who were strolling right in front of her and Cyril, was unable to completely dampen the shimmer of her bright hopes. All the same, she was not so detached from earthly matters that she failed to observe how Rowena’s manner of walking was unequivocally clumsy.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0013 }

“However, I imagine her face is all that Hugh sees. That is so typical of a man,” Nell mused with contempt.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0014 }

“Will you be at home on Saturday afternoon?” Cyril inquired.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0015 }

“Yes.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0016 }

“Your presence will soon be sought by my mother and sisters,” Cyril remarked softly.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0017 }

A sensation went through Nell that could perhaps be called a thrill, though it was scarcely an agreeable one. None of Cyril’s family had ever been met by her; the importance of what he said was realized by her; and it possessed, in some way, an unalterable quality that gave her a chill.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0018 }

“I shall be glad to see them,” she stated without emotion; and then she questioned whether she actually would be glad. Naturally, she should be. Yet would it not prove to be a bit of a trial? Rumors had reached Nell concerning how the Gardners regarded the “infatuation” of their son and brother. Cyril had surely exercised some influence to arrange this visit. Nell was aware she would be scrutinized. From their agreement to visit, she gathered that, whether voluntarily or involuntarily, they considered her a potential addition to their family.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0019 }

“I will simply be who I am. I will not attempt to leave a favorable impression,” Nell reflected with superiority. However, she was pondering which dress it would be wiser to put on Saturday afternoon, as well as whether the recent fashion of piling her hair up would be more becoming to her than the previous manner; and the excursion on foot was somewhat ruined as far as she was concerned. When evening arrived, she had come to the conclusion that she would put on her brown chiffon come Saturday, yet she would arrange her hair in a low style.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0020 }

On Friday afternoon, none of the girls at Wexcombe had classes. Taking advantage of the occasion, Mabel was composing an essay intended for the Philomathic Society; she occupied a seat at the corner table in the living room, surrounded by a messy scatter of manuscript pages and notes upon the floor. Mabel consistently maintained that she was incapable of writing anything without tossing every page to the ground upon finishing it. Positioned directly in the center of the floor, Nell—attired in a serge skirt and flannel blouse, her hair somewhat ruffled by the breezy stroll back—was playing with the Sarah-cat using a wishbone. Snuggled together in her lap were both Smudge and Joseph. Because Honora was preparing food in the kitchen, a cozy scent of plums pervaded the entire home. Shortly afterward, draped in a massive work apron and bearing a mark of flour on her nose, she entered to display to Aunt Euphemia the chocolate cake that she had recently iced.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0021 }

At this favorable juncture there came a knock at the door. No person gave it a thought except Cressy, who jumped to her feet and answered it, anticipating a messenger delivering the headwear she had purchased earlier that day. Positioned on the doorstep were Mrs. Lisle and her daughters.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0022 }

Somehow managing to scramble to her feet, Nell dumped a pair of outraged cats from her lap while automatically moving her wishbone into her left hand from her right. Having to traverse the room to get to the kitchen door, Honora panicked, frantically shoved the chocolate cake beneath a cushion on the inglenook sofa, and bolted up the stairs. Mabel started frantically collecting her manuscript. Solely Aunt Euphemia and Cressy stayed composed. Owing to their efforts, all were shortly seated comfortably, Nell included. Honora descended, stripped of her apron and free of smudges, Mabel restored her corner to order, and Cressy rescued the moment with a torrent of prompt small talk.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0023 }

An elegant, slender, and attractive woman, Mrs. Lisle was impeccably dressed, displaying a friendliness that appeared slightly strained. A youthful version of her mother, Aline Lisle possessed none of that friendliness. Her efforts to be pleasant resulted merely in an arrogant and condescending demeanor. Dorothy Lisle was slender, cheerful, and somewhat boyish. Recognizing that she was the sister Cyril preferred, Nell felt drawn to her. Had her lively hazel eyes been dreamy dark ones, she would have closely resembled Cyril. Owing to her and Cressy, the visit actually proceeded quite smoothly, apart from a minor feeling of tension in the room and a pair of somewhat unfortunate events. Allowed to run free, Smudge and Joseph initiated a game of tag, leaping wildly onto Mrs. Lisle’s silk-clad lap and off again during their frantic dash. Mrs. Lisle raised her lorgnette and watched their retreating shapes as though felines were entirely foreign to her, while Nell, stifling somewhat anxious laughter, offered the best apology she could manage.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0024 }

“Are you keen on cats?” inquired Mrs. Lisle, her tone carrying a subtle hint of indulgent surprise.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0025 }

Even though she cared for Smudge, Nell did not particularly care for cats, yet the manner of Mrs. Lisle’s speaking irked her. Irrationally, it came to her mind that Mrs. John Carrow held such a fondness for cats that her home contained every one her spouse permitted.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0026 }

“Aren’t they adorable animals?” she asked mischievously.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0027 }

“Cats have never been to my liking,” Mrs. Lisle said distantly.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0028 }

“I love them,” Dorothy said. “They possess such a wonderful selfishness. Dogs show too much goodness and selflessness. They cause me to feel uneasy. Cats, however, are magnificently human.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0029 }

“You have two delightful old china dogs there. May I look at them closely?” said Aline, moving across the room to the fireplace and thus unwittingly causing the next mishap. Taking up Magog, she took a seat on the cushion that hid Honora’s chocolate cake beneath it. Agonized glances were shared between Honora and Nell, yet they were helpless. Sitting on the cushion, the majestic Aline kept talking about china dogs right up to the moment she left.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0030 }

Dorothy stayed behind for a second so she could press the hand of Nell and utter a sudden whisper.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0031 }

“I am certain you and I will become good friends. Ah, Cyril has filled me in on everything concerning you. Poor lad, I am the sole family member he opens up to—after all, no one is able to entrust secrets to mamma and Aline. What marvelous experiences you girls are sure to enjoy in this place! Will you allow me to visit frequently and participate in them?”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0032 }

“Visit as frequently as you wish,” Nell answered warmly, grateful that a single sister of Cyril’s proved agreeable. She could never feel affection for Aline, of that she was sure; nor would Aline ever care for her, even if Mrs. Lisle could perhaps be gained over. On the whole, Nell let out a sigh of release once the trial had ended.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0033 }

“‘Out of every melancholy phrase expressed by voice or quill, none carry more sorrow than it might have been,’”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0034 }

lamented Honora in a tragic tone, raising the pillow. “What we have here in this cake is what one could term an utter collapse. Furthermore, the pillow has also been destroyed. Don't ever try to convince me that Friday isn't an unpropitious day.”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0035 }

“Those who announce their arrival for Saturday ought not to show up on Friday,” Aunt Euphemia remarked.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0036 }

“I believe Cyril made a blunder,” Cressy remarked. “The lad truly cannot be held accountable for his words while speaking with Nell. What has become of Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0037 }

Nell had walked up to the higher floor. A strange sensation made her want to weep. However, she forced a laugh from herself rather than shedding tears. Smudge and Joseph had behaved so terribly! Furthermore, Dorothy was truly a sweetheart.
{: #nw-v03-c36-p0038 }
